subject: Biology
title: Animal Kingdom
summary: The chapter first fixes the six characters on which all animals are sorted (level of organisation, symmetry, germ layers, coelom, segmentation, notochord) and then walks through the eleven phyla in order, from sponges to chordates, and the seven vertebrate classes. It is the most fact-dense chapter of Class 11: the examiner asks for the exact NCERT feature, the exact NCERT example and the exact NCERT word (choanocyte, cnidoblast, flame cell, nephridia, Malpighian tubule, radula, water vascular system), and the same facts return in NEET every year.

exam_profile.weightage: Class 11 Biology is a 70-mark theory paper set by the school on the CBSE pattern. Animal Kingdom belongs to Unit I, Diversity of Living World, which carries 15 marks shared with The Living World, Biological Classification and Plant Kingdom. In a typical school final this chapter alone contributes about 5 to 7 marks: two or three 1-mark items (an MCQ, a match-the-column or an Assertion–Reason), a 2-mark differentiation, a 3-mark salient-features question and often one 5-mark question on the basis of classification or on a phylum with a labelled diagram. In NEET it is among the highest-yielding chapters, with three to five questions almost every year, nearly all taken directly from NCERT tables and examples.

question_types.note: Match an example to its phylum or class (Pleurobrachia, Aplysia, Balanoglossus, Ichthyophis, Ornithorhynchus, Limulus); the excretory organ of a phylum (flame cells, nephridia, Malpighian tubules, proboscis gland); which phylum first shows a true coelom, a complete gut, segmentation, an open or closed circulation; which fish has no air bladder; which reptile has a four-chambered heart; the ploidy-free but memory-heavy 'odd one out' among examples.

Cartilaginous fishes swim constantly because they lack an air bladder; echinoderms are placed with bilateral animals because the larva is bilateral; Hemichordata is a separate phylum because the stomochord is not a true notochord; all vertebrates are chordates but not the reverse; birds have pneumatic bones for flight; Aschelminthes are pseudocoelomates because mesoderm is present only as scattered pouches.

Define metagenesis, metameric segmentation, pseudocoelom, water vascular system; distinguish polyp from medusa, direct from indirect development, intracellular from extracellular digestion, open from closed circulation, oviparous from viviparous; name two examples each of a given phylum or class; the three fundamental characters of chordates.

Salient features of a named phylum with two examples; the canal system of sponges; why Arthropoda is the largest phylum; the adaptations of birds for flight; the peculiar features of parasitic platyhelminthes; three differences between Chondrichthyes and Osteichthyes; between chordates and non-chordates.

Describe the basis of animal classification (levels of organisation, symmetry, germ layers, coelom, segmentation, notochord) with diagrams; the classification of phylum Chordata down to the classes with one example each; a comparison of the five vertebrate classes (heart chambers, skin, fertilisation, temperature regulation); phylum Arthropoda or Mollusca in full.

A passage on a specimen description (a marine animal with comb plates, a worm with a proboscis and collar, a fish without operculum) followed by four sub-questions asking for the phylum, a defining feature, an example and a comparison; or a passage on the coelom followed by classification of named animals.

hot_topics: Basis of classification: levels of organisation, symmetry, diploblastic vs triploblastic, coelom types, segmentation, notochord
Phylum Porifera: canal system, choanocytes, spicules, examples
Coelenterata: cnidoblasts, polyp and medusa, metagenesis in Obelia
Excretory organs across phyla: flame cells, nephridia, Malpighian tubules, proboscis gland, kidneys
Arthropoda as the largest phylum and its economically important examples
Echinodermata: water vascular system, radial adult and bilateral larva
Chordata: three fundamental characters, protochordates, all vertebrates are chordates
Chondrichthyes vs Osteichthyes; heart chambers and temperature regulation across vertebrate classes

sections.heading: Introduction and 4.1.1 Levels of organisation
sections.body:
Over a million animal species have been described, and new ones are added every year. Two things are true of them at once: they differ enormously in form, and yet they share a small set of fundamental features. The chapter is built on that second fact. If we sort animals by a few common characters, cell organisation, body symmetry, the nature of the coelom, the patterns of the digestive, circulatory and reproductive systems, the whole kingdom falls into eleven phyla, and any new specimen can be placed by asking the same questions in the same order. NCERT exercise 1 asks what would go wrong without such fundamental features: every species would have to be studied separately, no generalisation would be possible, and a new animal could not be related to any known group.

The first character is the level of organisation. Sponges show the cellular level: their cells are arranged as loose aggregates, with some division of labour but no tissues. Coelenterates reach the tissue level: cells performing the same function are arranged into tissues. Platyhelminthes and the higher phyla reach the organ level, where tissues are grouped into organs, each specialised for one function. Annelids, arthropods, molluscs, echinoderms and chordates show the organ system level: organs are associated to form functional systems, each concerned with one physiological function.

NCERT immediately adds that organ systems show further patterns worth noting. The digestive system may be incomplete, with a single opening serving as both mouth and anus (Platyhelminthes), or complete, with two openings, a mouth and an anus. The circulatory system may be open, in which blood pumped out of the heart bathes the cells and tissues directly (arthropods, most molluscs), or closed, in which blood is circulated through a series of vessels of varying diameters, arteries, veins and capillaries (annelids, chordates). These three pairs of words, cellular to organ-system, incomplete versus complete, open versus closed, are the most frequently asked 1-mark items from the opening pages.

formulas.expr: Levels of organisation: cellular (Porifera) → tissue (Coelenterata, Ctenophora) → organ (Platyhelminthes) → organ system (Aschelminthes to Chordata)
where: one opening, mouth serves as anus too: Platyhelminthes (also Coelenterata)
two openings, mouth and anus: Aschelminthes onwards
blood leaves the heart and bathes cells directly: Arthropoda, Mollusca, Hemichordata
blood stays inside vessels: Annelida, Cephalochordata and Vertebrata

sections.tip: When asked 'level of organisation of Hydra', write tissue level, not organ level; when asked for sponges write cellular level. Students lose the mark by writing 'multicellular', which is not a level of organisation.

sections.heading: 4.1.2 Symmetry and 4.1.3 Diploblastic and triploblastic organisation
sections.body:
Symmetry is decided by asking how many planes can divide the animal into identical halves. Sponges are mostly asymmetrical: no plane passing through the centre divides them into equal halves. In radial symmetry, any plane passing through the central axis divides the organism into two identical halves; this is seen in coelenterates, ctenophores and adult echinoderms. In bilateral symmetry, only one plane (the sagittal plane, through the mid-line) produces identical left and right halves; annelids, arthropods and all the higher phyla are bilateral. Radial symmetry suits a sessile or drifting animal that meets its environment from all sides; bilateral symmetry goes with directed movement and a head end. Echinoderms are the classic trap: the adult is radial but the larva is bilateral, which is why the phylum is kept with the bilateral, triploblastic, coelomate animals.

Germ layers are the second character on this page. Animals in which the cells are arranged in two embryonic layers, an external ectoderm and an internal endoderm, are diploblastic. Between the two lies an undifferentiated jelly-like layer, the mesoglea, which is not a third germ layer. Coelenterates and ctenophores are diploblastic. Animals in which the developing embryo has a third germinal layer, the mesoderm, between the ectoderm and endoderm are triploblastic; Platyhelminthes onwards, up to the chordates, are triploblastic. Mesoderm is what makes muscles, a coelom and true organs possible, so the diploblastic to triploblastic step is the biggest jump in complexity in the chapter.

NCERT Figure 4.1 (radial and bilateral symmetry) and Figure 4.2 (a cross-section showing ectoderm, mesoglea and endoderm in a diploblastic animal beside ectoderm, mesoderm and endoderm in a triploblastic one) are asked as 'draw and label' items, and a 2-mark question often asks you to define both symmetries with one example each.

formulas.expr: Asymmetrical: Porifera. Radial: Coelenterata, Ctenophora, adult Echinodermata. Bilateral: Platyhelminthes onwards (and echinoderm larvae)
where: any plane through the central axis gives identical halves
only one plane gives identical halves

formulas.expr: Diploblastic: ectoderm + endoderm with mesoglea between (Coelenterata, Ctenophora). Triploblastic: ectoderm + mesoderm + endoderm (Platyhelminthes to Chordata)
where: undifferentiated, non-cellular jelly; not a germ layer

sections.tip: Write 'mesoglea' for diploblastic animals and 'mesoderm' for triploblastic ones; swapping the two words costs the whole mark.

sections.heading: 4.1.4 Coelom
sections.body:
The coelom is the body cavity that lies between the body wall and the gut wall and is lined by mesoderm. Whether such a cavity is present, and how it is lined, is 'very important in classification', as NCERT puts it, and exercise 3 asks exactly this. Three conditions exist.

Coelomates have a true coelom, lined on both sides by mesoderm: the outer (parietal) mesoderm lines the body wall and the inner (visceral) mesoderm covers the gut. Annelids, molluscs, arthropods, echinoderms, hemichordates and chordates are coelomates. Pseudocoelomates have a body cavity that is not lined by mesoderm; instead the mesoderm is present as scattered pouches between the ectoderm and endoderm, and the cavity is called a pseudocoelom. Aschelminthes (roundworms) are the pseudocoelomates. Acoelomates have no body cavity at all; the space between the body wall and the gut is filled with mesodermal cells (parenchyma). Platyhelminthes are acoelomates.

The coelom matters functionally too. It provides room for organs to grow and move independently of the body wall, a fluid-filled space that works as a hydrostatic skeleton in worms, and a route for transport of materials. Because it is a mesodermal structure it appears only in triploblastic animals, so diploblastic coelenterates are neither coelomate nor acoelomate in the strict NCERT scheme; the question is asked only from Platyhelminthes upward.

NCERT Figure 4.3 shows three cross-sections, coelomate, pseudocoelomate and acoelomate, with the mesoderm (usually shaded) in different positions. In the coelomate section the shaded mesoderm lines both the outside of the gut and the inside of the body wall, with the coelom between; in the pseudocoelomate section the shaded patches touch the body wall only and the cavity has no mesodermal lining on the gut side; in the acoelomate section the shading fills the whole space. Draw this figure for any 5-mark 'basis of classification' answer.

formulas.expr: Coelom = body cavity lined by mesoderm
where: Annelida, Arthropoda, Mollusca, Echinodermata, Hemichordata, Chordata
Aschelminthes: cavity not lined by mesoderm, mesoderm as scattered pouches

sections.tip: The one-line definition the examiner looks for is 'body cavity lined by mesoderm'. If you write only 'body cavity' you have described a pseudocoelom too, and the mark goes.

sections.heading: 4.1.5 Segmentation and 4.1.6 Notochord
sections.body:
Segmentation. In some animals the body is externally and internally divided into segments, with a serial repetition of at least some organs. NCERT's example is the earthworm, where the body shows this pattern, called metameric segmentation, and the phenomenon is known as metamerism. Each segment (metamere) carries its own pair of nephridia, its own ganglia and its own set of muscles, so the body is built of repeated units. Metamerism first appears in phylum Annelida (NCERT exercise 13, option c), and continues in Arthropoda and Chordata; the superficial rings on a tapeworm (proglottids) are not true metameres because they are budded off from the neck and do not share a repeated organ plan, which is why Platyhelminthes is the wrong option in that exercise.

Notochord. The notochord is a mesodermally derived, rod-like structure formed on the dorsal side during embryonic development in some animals. Animals with a notochord are called chordates; animals without it are non-chordates, and NCERT lists Porifera to Echinodermata (and Hemichordata) as non-chordates. In vertebrates the notochord is present only in the embryo and is later replaced by the vertebral column; in Cephalochordata (Branchiostoma) it persists for life from head to tail; in Urochordata it is confined to the larval tail. All of this returns in section 4.2.11.

With these six characters in hand, NCERT's Figure 4.5 gives the broad classification: Kingdom Animalia splits into Non-chordates (ten phyla: Porifera, Coelenterata/Cnidaria, Ctenophora, Platyhelminthes, Aschelminthes, Annelida, Arthropoda, Mollusca, Echinodermata, Hemichordata) and phylum Chordata, which has three subphyla (Urochordata, Cephalochordata, Vertebrata). Vertebrata splits into Agnatha (class Cyclostomata) and Gnathostomata; Gnathostomata into Pisces (Chondrichthyes, Osteichthyes) and Tetrapoda (Amphibia, Reptilia, Aves, Mammalia). Exercise 2 ('If you are given a specimen, what steps would you follow to classify it?') expects you to apply the six characters in order and then move down this chart.

formulas.expr: Metameric segmentation: body divided externally and internally into segments with serial repetition of some organs; first seen in Annelida
Notochord: mesodermal, rod-like, dorsal, formed during embryonic development; present = chordate, absent = non-chordate
where: notochord only in the larval tail
notochord head to tail throughout life
notochord in embryo, replaced by vertebral column

sections.tip: For exercise 2 write the questions in order: level of organisation, symmetry, germ layers, coelom, segmentation, notochord, then name the phylum. A list of random features earns little.

sections.heading: 4.2.1 Phylum Porifera
sections.body:
Members of Porifera are commonly known as sponges. They are generally marine and mostly asymmetrical. They are primitive multicellular animals with the cellular level of organisation. The defining feature is the water transport or canal system: water enters through minute pores, the ostia, in the body wall, passes into a central cavity called the spongocoel, and leaves through a single large opening, the osculum. This one-way current does three jobs at once: gathering food, respiratory exchange and removal of waste. The spongocoel and the canals are lined by choanocytes or collar cells, flagellated cells whose beating drives the current and whose collars trap food particles. Digestion is intracellular; there is no gut. The body is supported by a skeleton made of spicules (calcareous or siliceous) or spongin fibres.

Reproduction: sponges are hermaphrodite, meaning eggs and sperms are produced by the same individual. They reproduce asexually by fragmentation and sexually by formation of gametes. Fertilisation is internal, and development is indirect, with a larval stage that is morphologically distinct from the adult. Examples to memorise exactly: Sycon (Scypha), Spongilla (fresh water sponge) and Euspongia (bath sponge). Spongilla is the exception to 'generally marine'; Euspongia is the one with a spongin skeleton used commercially.

Why examiners like sponges: the canal system is a ready 3-mark question ('describe the water transport system of sponges and mention its functions'), 'choanocytes' is a permanent match-the-column entry (exercise 14), and 'intracellular digestion' links to exercise 4. The word 'ostia' is the plural (singular ostium); write the plural for the pores.

formulas.expr: Porifera: marine, asymmetrical, cellular level, ostia → spongocoel → osculum, choanocytes, intracellular digestion, spicules or spongin
where: hermaphrodite; asexual by fragmentation, sexual by gametes; internal fertilisation; indirect development
Sycon (Scypha), Spongilla (fresh water sponge), Euspongia (bath sponge)

sections.tip: Three functions of the canal system, food gathering, respiratory exchange and waste removal, are three marking points. List all three.

sections.heading: 4.2.2 Phylum Coelenterata (Cnidaria)
sections.body:
Coelenterates are aquatic, mostly marine, sessile or free-swimming, radially symmetrical animals. The name Cnidaria comes from the cnidoblasts or cnidocytes, cells that contain the stinging capsules or nematocysts and are present on the tentacles and the body. Cnidoblasts are used for anchorage, defence and capture of prey. Cnidarians show the tissue level of organisation and are diploblastic. They have a central gastro-vascular cavity with a single opening, the mouth, on the hypostome. Digestion is both extracellular and intracellular: food is broken down first in the cavity by enzymes, and the pieces are then engulfed by cells of the lining. Some cnidarians, the corals, have a skeleton composed of calcium carbonate; coral reefs are built of it.

Cnidarians exhibit two basic body forms. The polyp is a sessile, cylindrical form, as in Hydra and Adamsia; the medusa is an umbrella-shaped, free-swimming form, as in Aurelia (the jelly fish). Cnidarians that exist in both forms show alternation of generation, called metagenesis: the polyps produce medusae asexually and the medusae form polyps sexually. NCERT's example is Obelia. Notice the exact direction: polyp gives medusa by asexual budding, medusa gives polyp through gametes. Both generations are diploid; metagenesis is not the same as the alternation of a haploid gametophyte and diploid sporophyte in plants, and an Assertion–Reason item tests exactly that difference.

Examples, with the common names NCERT attaches: Physalia (Portuguese man-of-war), Adamsia (sea anemone), Pennatula (sea-pen), Gorgonia (sea-fan), Meandrina (brain coral), and from the figures Aurelia (medusa) and Hydra. A 3-mark 'salient features of Coelenterata' answer should carry cnidoblasts, tissue level, diploblastic, gastro-vascular cavity with one opening, both kinds of digestion, polyp and medusa, and two examples.

formulas.expr: Cnidaria: aquatic, radial, tissue level, diploblastic, cnidoblasts with nematocysts, gastro-vascular cavity with one opening on hypostome, digestion extracellular + intracellular
where: Obelia: polyps form medusae asexually, medusae form polyps sexually

sections.tip: Physalia is the Portuguese man-of-war (a colonial cnidarian), not a mollusc, and Pennatula is the sea-pen, not a plant; both appear as odd-one-out MCQs.

sections.heading: 4.2.3 Phylum Ctenophora
sections.body:
Ctenophores are commonly known as sea walnuts or comb jellies. They are exclusively marine, radially symmetrical, diploblastic organisms with the tissue level of organisation. The body bears eight external rows of ciliated comb plates, which help in locomotion; the comb plates are the 'ctenes' that give the phylum its name and the entry 'comb plates → Ctenophora' in NCERT exercise 14. Digestion is both extracellular and intracellular, as in cnidarians. Bioluminescence, the property of a living organism to emit light, is well-marked in ctenophores; this is the fact NCERT chooses to mention, and it is the MCQ the examiner chooses to set.

Reproduction: sexes are not separate (they are hermaphrodite); reproduction takes place only by sexual means, fertilisation is external, and development is indirect. Examples: Pleurobrachia and Ctenoplana.

The phylum is small in NCERT but rich in contrasts with Cnidaria, and a 2-mark 'distinguish between Coelenterata and Ctenophora' is common. Ctenophores have no cnidoblasts, move with comb plates rather than by muscular contraction or medusa pulsing, show no polyp-medusa alternation, and are exclusively marine while some cnidarians (Hydra) are fresh-water. Both are radial, diploblastic and at the tissue level with a gastro-vascular cavity. If a question asks for a diploblastic animal that is not a cnidarian, Pleurobrachia is the answer.

formulas.expr: Ctenophora: exclusively marine, radial, diploblastic, tissue level, 8 rows of ciliated comb plates, bioluminescence, digestion extracellular + intracellular
where: sexes not separate; sexual only; external fertilisation; indirect development

sections.tip: Write 'eight rows of ciliated comb plates'; the number eight is a marking point.

sections.heading: 4.2.4 Phylum Platyhelminthes
sections.body:
Platyhelminthes have a dorso-ventrally flattened body, hence the name flatworms. They are mostly endoparasites found in animals including human beings. They are bilaterally symmetrical, triploblastic and acoelomate with the organ level of organisation. Three features follow from the parasitic habit, and together they answer NCERT exercise 6: hooks and suckers are present in the parasitic forms for attachment to the host; some of them absorb nutrients from the host directly through their body surface, so a gut may be reduced or absent (the tapeworm has none); and the body is flat so that every cell is close enough to the surface for exchange without a circulatory system. The digestive system, where present, is incomplete (single opening).

Excretion and osmoregulation are performed by specialised cells called flame cells, the first entry in the excretory-organ sequence that the examiner loves to test (flame cells, nephridia, Malpighian tubules, proboscis gland, kidneys). Flatworms are hermaphrodite; fertilisation is internal and development is through many larval stages. Planaria possesses a high regeneration capacity, a fact that appears as a 1-mark item. Examples: Taenia (tapeworm) and Fasciola (liver fluke).

For a 3-mark salient-features answer include: flat body, endoparasitic habit, bilateral, triploblastic, acoelomate, organ level, hooks and suckers, flame cells, hermaphrodite with internal fertilisation and larval stages, and two examples. Exercise 15 (animals parasitic on humans) draws on this phylum (Taenia solium, Fasciola hepatica) together with Aschelminthes (Ascaris, Wuchereria, Ancylostoma), Annelida (Hirudinaria, an ectoparasite) and Arthropoda (mosquitoes, lice, bed bugs as ectoparasites and vectors).

formulas.expr: Platyhelminthes: dorso-ventrally flat, mostly endoparasites, bilateral, triploblastic, acoelomate, organ level, hooks and suckers, flame cells, hermaphrodite, internal fertilisation, many larval stages

sections.tip: Exercise 6 asks for 'peculiar features' of parasitic platyhelminthes: hooks and suckers, direct absorption through the body surface, and the flattened body. Do not answer it with the general features of the phylum.

sections.heading: 4.2.5 Phylum Aschelminthes
sections.body:
The body of aschelminthes is circular in cross-section, hence the name roundworms. They may be free-living, aquatic and terrestrial, or parasitic in plants and animals. Roundworms show the organ-system level of body organisation. They are bilaterally symmetrical, triploblastic and pseudocoelomate: the body cavity is not lined by mesoderm. The alimentary canal is complete, with a well-developed muscular pharynx, so Aschelminthes is the first phylum in NCERT order with a complete digestive tract (mouth and anus). An excretory tube removes body wastes from the body cavity through the excretory pore.

Sexes are separate (dioecious), and females are often longer than males: this sexual dimorphism is why NCERT figures Ascaris as separate male and female worms, the male smaller with a curved posterior end. Fertilisation is internal, and development may be direct (the young resemble the adult) or indirect. Examples: Ascaris (round worm), Wuchereria (filaria worm, the cause of elephantiasis) and Ancylostoma (hookworm). All three are human parasites and belong in the exercise 15 list.

Compare with the flatworms to score the 2-mark differentiation: flatworms are flat, acoelomate, hermaphrodite, with an incomplete gut and flame cells; roundworms are cylindrical, pseudocoelomate, dioecious, with a complete gut and an excretory tube. Note the phylum name too: the rationalised NCERT still calls the phylum Aschelminthes (the older name Nematoda is not used in the text, though some papers use it).

formulas.expr: Aschelminthes: circular in cross-section, free-living or parasitic, organ-system level, bilateral, triploblastic, pseudocoelomate, complete gut with muscular pharynx, excretory tube with excretory pore
where: separate; females often longer than males; internal fertilisation; direct or indirect development

sections.tip: First phylum with a complete alimentary canal and the only pseudocoelomate phylum in NCERT: two MCQ answers in one line.

sections.heading: 4.2.6 Phylum Annelida
sections.body:
Annelids may be aquatic (marine and fresh water) or terrestrial, free-living and sometimes parasitic. They exhibit the organ-system level of organisation and are bilaterally symmetrical, triploblastic, metamerically segmented and coelomate. Their body surface is distinctly marked out into segments or metameres (Latin annulus, little ring), and this is the first phylum to show true metamerism and the first with a true coelom. They possess longitudinal and circular muscles which help in locomotion, working against the coelomic fluid as a hydrostatic skeleton. Aquatic annelids like Nereis possess lateral appendages, the parapodia, which help in swimming (exercise 14: parapodia → Annelida).

A closed circulatory system is present, the first in NCERT order. Nephridia help in osmoregulation and excretion (the second entry in the excretory-organ series, after flame cells). The neural system consists of paired ganglia connected by lateral nerves to a double ventral nerve cord, which is the non-chordate plan that Table 4.1 contrasts with the single, dorsal, hollow nerve cord of chordates.

Reproduction: Nereis is dioecious (sexes separate), but earthworms and leeches are monoecious (hermaphrodite). Reproduction is sexual. Examples: Nereis, Pheretima (earthworm) and Hirudinaria (blood-sucking leech). Hirudinaria is an ectoparasite and is the 'parasitic' annelid NCERT has in mind. The 3-mark salient-features question here usually asks you to underline what appears first: metameric segmentation, true coelom and closed circulation.

formulas.expr: Annelida: aquatic or terrestrial, organ-system level, bilateral, triploblastic, metamerically segmented, coelomate, longitudinal + circular muscles, closed circulation, nephridia, paired ganglia with double ventral nerve cord
where: lateral appendages of Nereis for swimming
Nereis dioecious; earthworm and leech monoecious; sexual reproduction

sections.tip: The examiner will accept 'Pheretima' or 'earthworm' but marks the nerve cord only if you write 'double ventral nerve cord'; a bare 'ventral nerve cord' is half the point.

sections.heading: 4.2.7 Phylum Arthropoda
sections.body:
This is the largest phylum of Animalia: it includes insects, and over two-thirds of all named species on earth are arthropods. They have the organ-system level of organisation, are bilaterally symmetrical, triploblastic, segmented and coelomate. The body is covered by a chitinous exoskeleton and consists of head, thorax and abdomen. They have jointed appendages (arthros, joint; poda, appendages), the character that names the phylum. Respiratory organs vary with habitat: gills (prawn), book gills (Limulus), book lungs (scorpion, spider) or a tracheal system (insects). The circulatory system is open. Sensory organs include antennae, eyes (compound and simple) and statocysts or balance organs. Excretion takes place through Malpighian tubules. They are mostly dioecious, fertilisation is usually internal, they are mostly oviparous, and development may be direct or indirect (indirect development in insects involves larval stages and metamorphosis).

NCERT groups the examples by importance, and the grouping itself is asked. Economically important insects: Apis (honey bee), Bombyx (silkworm), Laccifer (lac insect). Vectors: Anopheles, Culex and Aedes (mosquitoes). Gregarious pest: Locusta (locust). Living fossil: Limulus (king crab). Figures also show a butterfly, a scorpion and a prawn.

Exercise 7 asks why arthropods form the largest group; the answer is a list of the reasons for their success: a tough chitinous exoskeleton that protects and prevents water loss, jointed appendages for varied locomotion and feeding, a small body size, wings and the power of flight in insects, a wide range of respiratory organs that allow every habitat, a high reproductive rate with internal fertilisation and protected eggs, well-developed sense organs, and metamorphosis that lets larva and adult use different food. Give at least four points for 3 marks.

formulas.expr: Arthropoda: largest phylum (>2/3 of named species), chitinous exoskeleton, head-thorax-abdomen, jointed appendages, open circulation, Malpighian tubules, antennae + compound/simple eyes + statocysts
where: gills, book gills, book lungs or tracheal system
mostly dioecious, internal fertilisation, mostly oviparous, direct or indirect development
Apis, Bombyx, Laccifer (economic); Anopheles, Culex, Aedes (vectors); Locusta (gregarious pest); Limulus (living fossil)

sections.tip: Limulus is the king crab and a living fossil, but it is an arthropod (a chelicerate), not a mollusc or a true crab; and statocysts are 'balance organs', the phrase the marking scheme carries.

sections.heading: 4.2.8 Phylum Mollusca
sections.body:
Mollusca is the second largest animal phylum. Molluscs are terrestrial or aquatic (marine or fresh water), with the organ-system level of organisation. They are bilaterally symmetrical, triploblastic and coelomate. The body is covered by a calcareous shell and is unsegmented, with a distinct head, a muscular foot and a visceral hump. A soft and spongy layer of skin forms a mantle over the visceral hump, and the space between the hump and the mantle is the mantle cavity, in which feather-like gills are present. The gills have both respiratory and excretory functions. The anterior head region has sensory tentacles. The mouth contains a file-like rasping organ for feeding, the radula (exercise 14: radula → Mollusca).

Reproduction: they are usually dioecious and oviparous, with indirect development. Examples, all of which have appeared as MCQ options: Pila (apple snail), Pinctada (pearl oyster), Sepia (cuttlefish), Loligo (squid), Octopus (devil fish), Aplysia (sea-hare), Dentalium (tusk shell), Chaetopleura (chiton).

Two contrasts are worth holding in mind. Annelida is segmented; Mollusca is unsegmented, though both are coelomate. Arthropoda has an exoskeleton of chitin; Mollusca has a shell of calcium carbonate secreted by the mantle. NCERT does not give the circulatory system for molluscs, but if a question expects it, most molluscs have an open circulatory system (cephalopods such as Octopus are the exception with a closed one). For a 3-mark answer write the six NCERT points: shell, unsegmented body with head-foot-visceral hump, mantle and mantle cavity, gills with two functions, tentacles, radula, and add reproduction and two examples.

formulas.expr: Mollusca: second largest phylum, calcareous shell, unsegmented, head + muscular foot + visceral hump, mantle and mantle cavity with feather-like gills (respiration + excretion), sensory tentacles, radula
where: Pila, Pinctada, Sepia, Loligo, Octopus, Aplysia, Dentalium, Chaetopleura

sections.tip: Aplysia (sea-hare) and Dentalium (tusk shell) are molluscs; students guess them as mammals or echinoderms in MCQs. Pinctada is the pearl oyster, the one with economic importance.

sections.heading: 4.2.9 Phylum Echinodermata
sections.body:
Echinoderms have an endoskeleton of calcareous ossicles, and hence the name (echinos, spiny; derma, skin), spiny bodied. Note the word endoskeleton: the plates lie under the skin, unlike the arthropod exoskeleton. All are marine, with the organ-system level of organisation. The adult echinoderms are radially symmetrical but the larvae are bilaterally symmetrical. They are triploblastic and coelomate. The digestive system is complete, with the mouth on the lower (ventral) side and the anus on the upper (dorsal) side.

The most distinctive feature is the water vascular system, which helps in locomotion, capture and transport of food, and respiration. Sea water enters through the madreporite, passes through canals and ends in the tube feet, which extend and retract hydraulically. This answers exercise 8 (water vascular system is the characteristic of echinoderms), and the three functions are three marking points. An excretory system is absent, so in the excretory-organ series the entry for Echinodermata is 'none'. Sexes are separate, reproduction is sexual, fertilisation is usually external, and development is indirect with a free-swimming larva.

Examples with common names: Asterias (star fish), Echinus (sea urchin), Antedon (sea lily), Cucumaria (sea cucumber), Ophiura (brittle star). The 'sea lily' name for Antedon is set as a trap in odd-one-out MCQs because it sounds like a plant. The Assertion–Reason favourite: echinoderms are grouped with bilateral animals although the adult is radial, because the larva is bilateral and the adult radial symmetry is secondary.

formulas.expr: Echinodermata: endoskeleton of calcareous ossicles, all marine, organ-system level, adult radial / larva bilateral, triploblastic, coelomate, complete gut (mouth ventral, anus dorsal), water vascular system, no excretory system
where: locomotion, capture and transport of food, respiration
sexes separate, external fertilisation, indirect development with free-swimming larva

sections.tip: Mouth ventral, anus dorsal, and 'excretory system absent' are the three details that separate a full-marks answer from a generic one.

sections.heading: 4.2.10 Phylum Hemichordata
sections.body:
Hemichordata was earlier considered a sub-phylum under phylum Chordata, but it is now placed as a separate phylum under non-chordata. The reason, which the Assertion–Reason item asks, is that the structure once taken for a notochord (the stomochord or buccal diverticulum in the proboscis) is not homologous to the true notochord. This phylum consists of a small group of worm-like marine animals with the organ-system level of organisation. They are bilaterally symmetrical, triploblastic and coelomate. The body is cylindrical and is composed of an anterior proboscis, a collar and a long trunk. These three regions are the labels expected on the diagram of Balanoglossus.

The circulatory system is open. Respiration takes place through gills (pharyngeal gill slits open in the trunk, which is one reason they were once placed with chordates). The excretory organ is the proboscis gland, the fourth entry in the excretory-organ series. Sexes are separate, fertilisation is external, and development is indirect (with a tornaria larva, though NCERT names only 'indirect development'). Examples: Balanoglossus and Saccoglossus.

The examiner's 2-mark question is 'Why is Hemichordata no longer placed under Chordata?' or 'Name the three body regions and the excretory organ of Balanoglossus'. Both are answered above. If a question lists non-chordate phyla, remember to include Hemichordata as the tenth, after Echinodermata.

formulas.expr: Hemichordata: worm-like marine, organ-system level, bilateral, triploblastic, coelomate, body = proboscis + collar + trunk, open circulation, gills, proboscis gland
where: earlier a sub-phylum of Chordata; now a separate non-chordate phylum
sexes separate, external fertilisation, indirect development

sections.tip: Proboscis gland is the excretory organ; do not write nephridia or flame cells for Balanoglossus.

sections.heading: 4.2.11 Phylum Chordata: fundamental characters, protochordates and Vertebrata
sections.body:
Animals belonging to phylum Chordata are fundamentally characterised by the presence of a notochord, a dorsal hollow nerve cord and paired pharyngeal gill slits. These three are 'the fundamental characters' and every chordate shows them at some stage of life. Chordates are bilaterally symmetrical, triploblastic, coelomate, with the organ-system level of organisation. They possess a post-anal tail and a closed circulatory system. NCERT's comparison table sets chordates against non-chordates on five rows, and a 3-mark comparison is a standard question: notochord present versus absent; central nervous system dorsal, hollow and single versus ventral, solid and double; pharynx perforated by gill slits versus not; heart ventral versus dorsal (if present); post-anal tail present versus absent.

Chordata is divided into three subphyla: Urochordata (Tunicata), Cephalochordata and Vertebrata. The first two are together called protochordates and are exclusively marine. In Urochordata the notochord is present only in the larval tail, and is lost in the sessile adult; in Cephalochordata it extends from head to tail region and is persistent throughout life. Examples: Urochordata, Ascidia, Salpa, Doliolum; Cephalochordata, Branchiostoma (Amphioxus or Lancelet).

Members of subphylum Vertebrata possess a notochord during the embryonic period; it is replaced by a cartilaginous or bony vertebral column in the adult. Thus all vertebrates are chordates but all chordates are not vertebrates (exercise 9): the protochordates keep the notochord and never build a vertebral column, so they are chordates without being vertebrates. Besides the basic chordate characters, vertebrates have a ventral muscular heart with two, three or four chambers, kidneys for excretion and osmoregulation, and paired appendages which may be fins or limbs. Vertebrata is divided into Agnatha (jawless; class Cyclostomata) and Gnathostomata (jawed), and Gnathostomata into superclass Pisces (bear fins: Chondrichthyes, Osteichthyes) and superclass Tetrapoda (bear limbs: Amphibia, Reptilia, Aves, Mammalia). Draw this chart for the 5-mark chordate classification question; it is the answer's skeleton.

formulas.expr: Chordata = notochord + dorsal hollow nerve cord + paired pharyngeal gill slits; plus post-anal tail, closed circulation, ventral heart
where: notochord only in larval tail: Ascidia, Salpa, Doliolum
notochord head to tail for life: Branchiostoma (Amphioxus, Lancelet)
notochord embryonic, replaced by vertebral column; ventral muscular heart (2, 3 or 4 chambers), kidneys, paired appendages

formulas.expr: Vertebrata → Agnatha (Cyclostomata) + Gnathostomata → Pisces (Chondrichthyes, Osteichthyes) + Tetrapoda (Amphibia, Reptilia, Aves, Mammalia)

sections.tip: Exercise 9 is a favourite. State the definition of each (chordate = has notochord; vertebrate = notochord replaced by vertebral column), then give protochordates as the chordates that are not vertebrates.

sections.heading: 4.2.11.1 Class Cyclostomata and 4.2.11.2 Class Chondrichthyes
sections.body:
Cyclostomata. All living members are ectoparasites on some fishes. They have an elongated body bearing 6 to 15 pairs of gill slits for respiration. Cyclostomes have a sucking and circular mouth without jaws (cyclo, circular; stoma, mouth), and they belong to Agnatha for that reason. The body is devoid of scales and paired fins. The cranium and vertebral column are cartilaginous. Circulation is of closed type. Cyclostomes are marine but migrate to fresh water for spawning; after spawning, within a few days, they die. Their larvae, after metamorphosis, return to the ocean. Examples: Petromyzon (lamprey) and Myxine (hagfish). Exercise 14 puts 'gill slits' against Cyclostomata and Chondrichthyes, the two groups whose gill slits are visible externally because there is no operculum.

Chondrichthyes. These are marine animals with a streamlined body and a cartilaginous endoskeleton. The mouth is located ventrally. The notochord is persistent throughout life. Gill slits are separate and without an operculum (gill cover). The skin is tough, containing minute placoid scales. Teeth are modified placoid scales which are backwardly directed; the jaws are very powerful, and these animals are predaceous. Because of the absence of an air bladder, they have to swim constantly to avoid sinking: that sentence is the answer to exercise 10 from the negative side and to the most common Assertion–Reason from this class. The heart is two-chambered (one auricle and one ventricle). Some of them have electric organs (Torpedo) and some possess a poison sting (Trygon). They are cold-blooded (poikilothermous), that is, they lack the capacity to regulate body temperature. Sexes are separate; in males the pelvic fins bear claspers. Fertilisation is internal, and many of them are viviparous. Examples: Scoliodon (dog fish), Pristis (saw fish), Carcharodon (great white shark), Trygon (sting ray).

formulas.expr: Cyclostomata: ectoparasites on fishes, 6–15 pairs of gill slits, circular jawless sucking mouth, no scales, no paired fins, cartilaginous cranium and vertebral column, closed circulation, marine but spawn in fresh water and die

Chondrichthyes: marine, cartilaginous endoskeleton, ventral mouth, notochord persistent, gill slits without operculum, placoid scales, teeth = modified placoid scales, no air bladder, 2-chambered heart, poikilothermous, claspers in male, internal fertilisation, many viviparous
where: Scoliodon (dog fish), Pristis (saw fish), Carcharodon (great white shark)

sections.tip: The male clasper is on the pelvic fin, the mouth is ventral, and the scales are placoid: three words that separate Chondrichthyes from Osteichthyes in every comparison table.

sections.heading: 4.2.11.3 Class Osteichthyes
sections.body:
Osteichthyes includes both marine and fresh water fishes with a bony endoskeleton. The body is streamlined, and the mouth is mostly terminal (compare the ventral mouth of sharks). They have four pairs of gills which are covered by an operculum on each side (exercise 14: operculum → Osteichthyes). The skin is covered with cycloid or ctenoid scales. The air bladder is present and regulates buoyancy, so bony fishes can hang at any depth without swimming; this is the positive side of exercise 10 ('how important is the presence of air bladder in Pisces'). The heart is two-chambered (one auricle and one ventricle), as in cartilaginous fishes; the two-chambered heart is a feature of all fishes. They are cold-blooded. Sexes are separate, fertilisation is usually external, they are mostly oviparous, and development is direct.

NCERT groups the examples by habitat and the grouping is asked. Marine: Exocoetus (flying fish), Hippocampus (sea horse). Fresh water: Labeo (rohu), Catla (katla), Clarias (magur). Aquarium: Betta (fighting fish), Pterophyllum (angel fish).

The 3-mark comparison between Chondrichthyes and Osteichthyes is one of the two or three most predictable questions in the chapter. Give it as a table with these rows: endoskeleton (cartilaginous versus bony), habitat (marine only versus marine and fresh water), mouth (ventral versus terminal), gill slits (separate, no operculum versus covered by operculum), scales (placoid versus cycloid or ctenoid), air bladder (absent versus present), fertilisation (internal versus external), reproduction (many viviparous versus mostly oviparous), and an example each (Scoliodon versus Labeo). Both classes share a two-chambered heart, cold-bloodedness and a streamlined body, so do not list those as differences.

formulas.expr: Osteichthyes: marine + fresh water, bony endoskeleton, terminal mouth, 4 pairs of gills under an operculum, cycloid/ctenoid scales, air bladder regulates buoyancy, 2-chambered heart, cold-blooded, external fertilisation, mostly oviparous, direct development

sections.tip: Hippocampus is a bony fish, not a mammal, and its habitat is marine; it appears in the odd-one-out MCQ almost every year.

sections.heading: 4.2.11.4 Class Amphibia and 4.2.11.5 Class Reptilia
sections.body:
Amphibia. As the name suggests (amphi, dual; bios, life), amphibians can live in aquatic as well as terrestrial habitats. Most have two pairs of limbs. The body is divisible into head and trunk; a tail may be present in some (Salamandra). The skin is moist and without scales, and it takes part in respiration. The eyes have eyelids. A tympanum represents the ear; there is no external ear. The alimentary canal, urinary and reproductive tracts open into a common chamber, the cloaca, which opens to the exterior. Respiration is by gills, lungs and through the skin. The heart is three-chambered (two auricles and one ventricle). They are cold-blooded. Sexes are separate, fertilisation is external, they are oviparous, and development is indirect (tadpole larva). Examples: Bufo (toad), Rana (frog), Hyla (tree frog), Salamandra (salamander), Ichthyophis (limbless amphibia). Ichthyophis is the MCQ favourite: limbless, but an amphibian, not a snake.

Reptilia. The class name refers to their creeping or crawling mode of locomotion (repere, to creep). They are mostly terrestrial, and the body is covered by dry and cornified skin with epidermal scales or scutes. They do not have external ear openings; the tympanum represents the ear. Limbs, when present, are two pairs. The heart is usually three-chambered, but four-chambered in crocodiles, the fact behind the most repeated reptile MCQ. Reptiles are poikilotherms. Snakes and lizards shed their scales as skin cast. Sexes are separate, fertilisation is internal, they are oviparous, and development is direct. Examples: Chelone (turtle), Testudo (tortoise), Chameleon (tree lizard), Calotes (garden lizard), Crocodilus (crocodile), Alligator, Hemidactylus (wall lizard), and the poisonous snakes Naja (cobra), Bangarus (krait), Vipera (viper).

The 2-mark differentiation between the two classes runs on skin (moist, scaleless versus dry, scaly), fertilisation (external versus internal), development (indirect versus direct) and respiration (skin and gills used versus lungs only). Both share a tympanum for an ear, a three-chambered heart (except crocodiles) and cold-bloodedness.

formulas.expr: Amphibia: aquatic + terrestrial, moist scaleless skin, eyelids, tympanum, cloaca, respiration by gills + lungs + skin, 3-chambered heart, cold-blooded, external fertilisation, oviparous, indirect development
where: Bufo (toad), Rana (frog), Hyla (tree frog), Salamandra (salamander), Ichthyophis (limbless amphibia)

formulas.expr: Reptilia: creeping locomotion, mostly terrestrial, dry cornified skin with epidermal scales or scutes, no external ear (tympanum), 3-chambered heart (4 in crocodiles), poikilotherm, skin cast in snakes and lizards, internal fertilisation, oviparous, direct development
where: Chelone, Testudo, Chameleon, Calotes, Crocodilus, Alligator, Hemidactylus, Naja, Bangarus, Vipera

sections.tip: Write 'usually three-chambered, four-chambered in crocodiles' for the reptile heart every time; the crocodile exception is the mark.

sections.heading: 4.2.11.6 Class Aves and 4.2.11.7 Class Mammalia
sections.body:
Aves. The characteristic features of birds are the presence of feathers and, in most, the ability to fly, though flightless birds such as the ostrich exist. They possess a beak. The forelimbs are modified into wings. The hind limbs generally have scales and are modified for walking, swimming or clasping tree branches. The skin is dry without glands except the oil gland at the base of the tail. The endoskeleton is fully ossified (bony) and the long bones are hollow with air cavities (pneumatic). The digestive tract has additional chambers, the crop and the gizzard. The heart is completely four-chambered. Birds are warm-blooded (homoiothermous): they maintain a constant body temperature. Respiration is by lungs, and air sacs connected to the lungs supplement respiration. Sexes are separate, fertilisation is internal, they are oviparous, and development is direct. Examples: Corvus (crow), Columba (pigeon), Psittacula (parrot), Struthio (ostrich), Pavo (peacock), Aptenodytes (penguin), Neophron (vulture). Exercise 11 (modifications for flight) is answered by picking the flight-related items out of this list: feathers, wings, pneumatic bones, air sacs, warm-bloodedness, a beak and no teeth (weight saving), and a streamlined body.

Mammalia. Mammals are found in a variety of habitats: polar ice caps, deserts, mountains, forests, grasslands and dark caves; some fly (bats) and some live in water (whales, dolphins). The most unique mammalian character is the presence of milk-producing glands (mammary glands) by which the young are nourished. They have two pairs of limbs adapted for walking, running, climbing, burrowing, swimming or flying. The skin is unique in possessing hair. External ears or pinnae are present (the only vertebrate class with them). Different types of teeth are present in the jaw (heterodont). The heart is four-chambered. They are homoiothermous. Respiration is by lungs. Sexes are separate, fertilisation is internal, they are viviparous with few exceptions, and development is direct. The exceptions are the oviparous mammals: Ornithorhynchus (platypus). Viviparous examples: Macropus (kangaroo), Pteropus (flying fox), Camelus (camel), Macaca (monkey), Rattus (rat), Canis (dog), Felis (cat), Elephas (elephant), Equus (horse), Delphinus (common dolphin), Balaenoptera (blue whale), Panthera tigris (tiger), Panthera leo (lion).

Exercise 12 asks whether an oviparous and a viviparous mother could produce equal numbers of young. No: the oviparous mother lays many eggs because the eggs are exposed to predators and the environment, so few survive; the viviparous mother nourishes a few young inside her body and gives them parental care, so survival is high and numbers are small.

formulas.expr: Aves: feathers, beak, forelimbs = wings, scaly hind limbs, dry skin with only an oil gland at tail base, pneumatic bones, crop + gizzard, 4-chambered heart, homoiothermous, lungs + air sacs, internal fertilisation, oviparous, direct development
where: Corvus, Columba, Psittacula, Struthio, Pavo, Aptenodytes, Neophron

formulas.expr: Mammalia: mammary glands, hair, pinnae, heterodont teeth, 4-chambered heart, homoiothermous, lungs, internal fertilisation, viviparous (except Ornithorhynchus), direct development
where: Macropus, Pteropus, Camelus, Macaca, Rattus, Canis, Felis, Elephas, Equus, Delphinus, Balaenoptera, Panthera tigris, Panthera leo

sections.tip: Pteropus is the flying fox, a bat, so a mammal; Aptenodytes is a penguin, so a bird; Delphinus and Balaenoptera are mammals though they live in water. These three lines settle most odd-one-out MCQs.

key_terms.definition: The simplest animal body plan, in which cells are arranged as loose aggregates with some division of labour but without tissues; seen in sponges.
Any plane passing through the central axis divides the body into two identical halves; seen in coelenterates, ctenophores and adult echinoderms.
Only one plane divides the body into identical left and right halves; seen in annelids, arthropods and all higher phyla.
Animals whose cells are arranged in two embryonic layers, an outer ectoderm and an inner endoderm, with an undifferentiated mesoglea between; coelenterates and ctenophores.
Animals with a third germinal layer, the mesoderm, between the ectoderm and endoderm; Platyhelminthes to Chordata.
A body cavity between the body wall and the gut that is lined by mesoderm; animals with it are coelomates.
A body cavity not lined by mesoderm, with the mesoderm present only as scattered pouches between ectoderm and endoderm; characteristic of Aschelminthes.
An animal with no body cavity, the space between body wall and gut being filled with mesodermal cells; Platyhelminthes.
Division of the body externally and internally into segments with serial repetition of at least some organs, as in the earthworm; first seen in Annelida.
A mesodermally derived rod-like structure formed on the dorsal side during embryonic development; its presence defines the chordates.
Flagellated cells that line the spongocoel and canals of sponges, driving the water current and trapping food.
Cells of cnidarians containing the stinging capsule or nematocyst, present on the tentacles and body and used for anchorage, defence and capture of prey.
Alternation of generation in cnidarians such as Obelia in which polyps produce medusae asexually and medusae form polyps sexually.
Specialised cells of Platyhelminthes that carry out osmoregulation and excretion.
The excretory and osmoregulatory organs of annelids, present in most segments.
The excretory organs of arthropods, opening into the gut.
A file-like rasping organ in the mouth of molluscs used for feeding.
The distinctive hydraulic canal system of echinoderms that helps in locomotion, capture and transport of food, and respiration.
The excretory organ of hemichordates such as Balanoglossus.
The two exclusively marine chordate subphyla, Urochordata and Cephalochordata, which have a notochord but no vertebral column.
The gill cover present on each side in bony fishes (Osteichthyes) and absent in cartilaginous fishes.
Minute tooth-like scales in the tough skin of Chondrichthyes; the teeth of sharks are modified placoid scales.
A common chamber into which the alimentary canal, urinary and reproductive tracts open, as in amphibians, which then opens to the exterior.
Hollow long bones with air cavities found in birds, which reduce weight for flight.
Cold-blooded animals that cannot regulate body temperature (fishes, amphibians, reptiles) versus warm-blooded animals that keep a constant body temperature (birds, mammals).
Egg-laying animals versus animals that give birth to young; among mammals only Ornithorhynchus is oviparous.

formula_sheet.name: Excretory organs across phyla
formula_sheet.expr: Platyhelminthes flame cells; Annelida nephridia; Arthropoda Malpighian tubules; Mollusca gills (also excretory); Echinodermata none; Hemichordata proboscis gland; Aschelminthes excretory tube and pore; Vertebrata kidneys
formula_sheet.note: The single most repeated matching item in the chapter

formula_sheet.name: Firsts in NCERT order
formula_sheet.expr: Tissue level: Coelenterata. Organ level and bilateral symmetry and triploblastic: Platyhelminthes. Complete gut and pseudocoelom: Aschelminthes. True coelom, metamerism, closed circulation: Annelida. Notochord: Chordata

formula_sheet.name: Circulatory system by phylum
formula_sheet.expr: Open: Arthropoda, Mollusca (most), Hemichordata. Closed: Annelida, Cephalochordata, Vertebrata (including Cyclostomata)
formula_sheet.note: Sponges, cnidarians, ctenophores, flatworms and roundworms have no circulatory system

formula_sheet.name: Digestion by phylum
formula_sheet.expr: Intracellular only: Porifera. Both extracellular and intracellular: Coelenterata, Ctenophora. Extracellular in a gut: Platyhelminthes onwards

formula_sheet.name: Heart chambers in vertebrates
formula_sheet.expr: Fishes (Chondrichthyes, Osteichthyes) 2; Amphibia 3; Reptilia 3 (crocodiles 4); Aves 4; Mammalia 4
formula_sheet.note: Cold-blooded up to Reptilia; warm-blooded Aves and Mammalia

formula_sheet.name: Fertilisation and development in vertebrate classes
formula_sheet.expr: Chondrichthyes internal, many viviparous. Osteichthyes external, oviparous, direct. Amphibia external, oviparous, indirect. Reptilia internal, oviparous, direct. Aves internal, oviparous, direct. Mammalia internal, viviparous (Ornithorhynchus oviparous), direct
formula_sheet.note: Amphibia is the only tetrapod class with external fertilisation and indirect development

formula_sheet.name: Sponge canal system
formula_sheet.expr: Ostia → spongocoel (lined by choanocytes) → osculum; functions: food gathering, respiratory exchange, removal of waste
formula_sheet.note: Skeleton of spicules or spongin fibres

formula_sheet.name: Cnidarian body forms
formula_sheet.expr: Polyp: sessile, cylindrical (Hydra, Adamsia). Medusa: umbrella-shaped, free-swimming (Aurelia). Metagenesis in Obelia: polyp → medusa asexually, medusa → polyp sexually
formula_sheet.note: Corals have a calcium carbonate skeleton

formula_sheet.name: Chordate fundamental characters
formula_sheet.expr: Notochord + dorsal hollow nerve cord + paired pharyngeal gill slits; also post-anal tail and closed circulation
formula_sheet.note: Non-chordates: notochord absent, CNS ventral solid double, pharynx not perforated, heart dorsal if present, no post-anal tail

formula_sheet.name: Notochord fate in the three subphyla
formula_sheet.expr: Urochordata: larval tail only (Ascidia, Salpa, Doliolum). Cephalochordata: head to tail for life (Branchiostoma). Vertebrata: embryonic, replaced by cartilaginous or bony vertebral column
formula_sheet.note: All vertebrates are chordates; not all chordates are vertebrates

formula_sheet.name: Chondrichthyes versus Osteichthyes
formula_sheet.expr: Cartilage vs bone; marine vs marine and fresh water; ventral vs terminal mouth; no operculum vs operculum; placoid vs cycloid or ctenoid scales; no air bladder vs air bladder; internal vs external fertilisation; many viviparous vs mostly oviparous

formula_sheet.name: Arthropod respiratory organs and example groups
formula_sheet.expr: Gills, book gills, book lungs, tracheal system. Apis, Bombyx, Laccifer (economic); Anopheles, Culex, Aedes (vectors); Locusta (gregarious pest); Limulus (living fossil)
formula_sheet.note: Largest phylum, over two-thirds of named species; sensory organs antennae, compound and simple eyes, statocysts

formula_sheet.name: Body regions
formula_sheet.expr: Arthropoda: head, thorax, abdomen. Mollusca: head, muscular foot, visceral hump (with mantle). Hemichordata: proboscis, collar, trunk. Amphibia: head and trunk
formula_sheet.note: Labels expected on the corresponding diagrams

formula_sheet.name: Reproduction quick facts
formula_sheet.expr: Hermaphrodite: Porifera, Ctenophora, Platyhelminthes, earthworm and leech. Dioecious: Aschelminthes (female longer), Nereis, Arthropoda (mostly), Mollusca (usually), Echinodermata, Hemichordata, all vertebrates
formula_sheet.note: Asexual reproduction only in Porifera (fragmentation) and cnidarian polyps (budding); Ctenophora sexual only

formula_sheet.name: Special one-liners
formula_sheet.expr: Bioluminescence: Ctenophora. Regeneration: Planaria. Electric organ: Torpedo. Poison sting: Trygon. Claspers: male Chondrichthyes. Four-chambered heart reptile: crocodile. Oviparous mammal: Ornithorhynchus. Limbless amphibian: Ichthyophis. Cyclostomes die after spawning

diagrams.title: Symmetry: radial and bilateral (NCERT Figure 4.1)
diagrams.how_to_draw: Draw two outlines side by side. Left: a starfish-like or round cnidarian body seen from above with three or four dotted lines passing through the centre, each dividing it into identical halves; caption 'radial symmetry, any plane through the central axis'. Right: a bilaterally symmetrical animal (a fish or a butterfly outline) with a single dotted mid-line from head to tail; caption 'bilateral symmetry, only one plane'. Label the plane(s), the central axis and the anterior end on the bilateral figure.

diagrams.title: Diploblastic and triploblastic organisation (NCERT Figure 4.2)
diagrams.how_to_draw: Two body-wall sections. Left (diploblastic): an outer band labelled ectoderm, an inner band labelled endoderm and a clear jelly layer between labelled mesoglea; caption Hydra or a coelenterate. Right (triploblastic): three bands labelled ectoderm, mesoderm and endoderm. Shade the mesoderm differently and state in the caption that mesoglea is not a germ layer while mesoderm is.

diagrams.title: Coelomate, pseudocoelomate and acoelomate (NCERT Figure 4.3)
diagrams.how_to_draw: Three transverse sections of a worm, each a ring (body wall) with a smaller ring (gut) inside. Coelomate: shade the mesoderm as a lining on the inside of the body wall and on the outside of the gut, leaving a clear coelom between; label ectoderm, mesoderm (parietal and visceral), endoderm, coelom, gut. Pseudocoelomate: shade the mesoderm only as patches against the body wall and leave the cavity unlined on the gut side; label pseudocoelom. Acoelomate: fill the whole space between body wall and gut with shaded mesoderm; label 'no body cavity'. Give one example under each: Annelida, Aschelminthes, Platyhelminthes.
