ncert_questions.q: What are the difficulties that you would face in classification of animals, if common fundamental features are not taken into account?
ncert_questions.a: Without common fundamental features, classification would have to rely on superficial features such as size, colour or habitat, which vary even within a species and are shared by unrelated animals. The consequences would be: (i) each of the more than a million species would have to be studied and described separately, with no grouping possible; (ii) animals with a common ancestry could not be placed together, so the system would not reflect evolutionary relationships; (iii) a newly found animal could not be assigned to any group or compared with known ones; (iv) generalisations about a group (for instance that all chordates have a notochord) would be impossible, making the study of animals unmanageable. Fundamental features such as level of organisation, symmetry, germ layers, coelom, segmentation and notochord are shared by whole groups and change little with the environment, which is why they are used.

ncert_questions.q: If you are given a specimen, what are the steps that you would follow to classify it?
ncert_questions.a: Examine the specimen for the fundamental characters in this order: (i) Level of organisation: are the cells loosely arranged (cellular, sponges), organised into tissues (coelenterates), organs (flatworms) or organ systems (higher phyla)? (ii) Symmetry: asymmetrical, radial or bilateral. (iii) Germ layers: diploblastic (ectoderm and endoderm with mesoglea) or triploblastic (mesoderm present). (iv) Coelom: acoelomate, pseudocoelomate or coelomate. (v) Segmentation: is the body metamerically segmented? (vi) Notochord: present (chordate) or absent (non-chordate). Then use the pattern of the digestive system (incomplete or complete), circulatory system (open or closed), respiratory and excretory organs and reproductive features (sexes, fertilisation, development) to place it in a phylum, and for chordates check the notochord's fate, jaws, fins or limbs, scales, heart chambers and temperature regulation to reach the class.

ncert_questions.q: How useful is the study of the nature of body cavity and coelom in the classification of animals?
ncert_questions.a: The coelom is a body cavity lined by mesoderm, and its presence or absence and nature is very important in classification. (i) Animals with a true mesoderm-lined cavity are coelomates: Annelida, Arthropoda, Mollusca, Echinodermata, Hemichordata and Chordata. (ii) Animals in which the cavity is not lined by mesoderm and the mesoderm is present only as scattered pouches between ectoderm and endoderm are pseudocoelomates: Aschelminthes. (iii) Animals with no body cavity are acoelomates: Platyhelminthes. Thus the coelom separates the triploblastic phyla into three grades, and it also correlates with the level of organisation: coelomates have well-developed organ systems, since the coelom gives space for organs to grow and move, a hydrostatic skeleton and a medium for transport. It is therefore one of the six fundamental characters used to sort the animal kingdom.

ncert_questions.q: Distinguish between intracellular and extracellular digestion.
ncert_questions.a: Intracellular digestion: food is taken into the cell (by phagocytosis) and digested inside food vacuoles by enzymes secreted within the cell; it occurs in sponges (choanocytes), and is combined with extracellular digestion in cnidarians and ctenophores. It limits the size of food that can be handled. Extracellular digestion: enzymes are released into a gut cavity (gastro-vascular cavity or alimentary canal) where food is broken down outside the cells and the products are then absorbed; it is found in coelenterates (in the gastro-vascular cavity) and in all higher animals from Platyhelminthes onwards, and allows large prey to be digested.

ncert_questions.q: What is the difference between direct and indirect development?
ncert_questions.a: Direct development: the young that hatches or is born resembles the adult in form, differing only in size and sexual maturity, and there is no larval stage; examples are Aschelminthes (in some), reptiles, birds and mammals. Indirect development: the embryo develops into a larva that is morphologically distinct from the adult and undergoes metamorphosis to reach the adult form; examples are sponges, cnidarians, echinoderms (free-swimming larva), insects (larva and pupa) and amphibians (tadpole). Indirect development lets the larva and the adult use different food and habitats.

ncert_questions.q: What are the peculiar features that you find in parasitic Platyhelminthes?
ncert_questions.a: (i) Hooks and suckers are present in the parasitic forms for firm attachment to the host tissues (the scolex of Taenia). (ii) Nutrients are absorbed directly through the body surface from the host, so the digestive system is reduced (Fasciola) or absent (Taenia). (iii) The body is dorso-ventrally flattened, increasing surface area for absorption and exchange. (iv) They are hermaphrodite, with internal fertilisation and development through many larval stages, which suits transfer between hosts and produces enormous numbers of offspring. (v) The body is covered by a tegument that resists the host's digestive enzymes.

ncert_questions.q: What are the reasons that you can think of for the arthropods to constitute the largest group of the animal kingdom?
ncert_questions.a: Arthropods make up over two-thirds of all named species because of a combination of adaptive features: (i) a chitinous exoskeleton that protects against injury, predators and water loss, letting them colonise land; (ii) jointed appendages modified for walking, swimming, feeding, sensing and defence; (iii) wings and flight in insects, which allow dispersal and escape; (iv) small body size, so many species can share one habitat; (v) varied respiratory organs, gills, book gills, book lungs and tracheae, suiting water and land; (vi) well-developed sense organs: antennae, compound and simple eyes, statocysts; (vii) high reproductive capacity with internal fertilisation, protected eggs and short life cycles; (viii) metamorphosis, so larvae and adults exploit different food and do not compete.

ncert_questions.q: Water vascular system is the characteristic of which group of the following: (a) Porifera (b) Ctenophora (c) Echinodermata (d) Chordata
ncert_questions.a: (c) Echinodermata. The water vascular system is the most distinctive feature of echinoderms such as Asterias; it helps in locomotion, capture and transport of food, and respiration.

ncert_questions.q: 'All vertebrates are chordates but all chordates are not vertebrates.' Justify the statement.
ncert_questions.a: A chordate is an animal that possesses, at some stage of life, a notochord, a dorsal hollow nerve cord and paired pharyngeal gill slits. A vertebrate is a chordate in which the notochord is present during the embryonic period and is replaced in the adult by a cartilaginous or bony vertebral column. Every vertebrate therefore has the chordate characters and is a chordate. But phylum Chordata also includes the protochordates, subphylum Urochordata (Ascidia, Salpa, Doliolum) and subphylum Cephalochordata (Branchiostoma), which retain the notochord (in the larval tail, or throughout life from head to tail) and never form a vertebral column. These animals are chordates but not vertebrates. Hence all vertebrates are chordates, but all chordates are not vertebrates.

ncert_questions.q: How important is the presence of air bladder in Pisces?
ncert_questions.a: The air bladder (swim bladder) is a gas-filled sac present in bony fishes (Osteichthyes) that regulates buoyancy. By adjusting the amount of gas in it the fish can remain at any depth without spending energy on swimming. Cartilaginous fishes (Chondrichthyes) lack an air bladder, and so they have to swim constantly to avoid sinking. The air bladder thus saves energy and allows a fish to hover, rise or sink at will; in some fishes it also assists respiration and sound production.

ncert_questions.q: What are the modifications that are observed in birds that help them fly?
ncert_questions.a: (i) Feathers covering the body, and the forelimbs modified into wings. (ii) Streamlined body with a light, toothless beak that reduces weight. (iii) Fully ossified endoskeleton with hollow, pneumatic long bones containing air cavities, giving strength with low weight. (iv) Air sacs connected to the lungs that supplement respiration and meet the high oxygen demand of flight. (v) A completely four-chambered heart and warm-bloodedness (homoiothermy), which sustain the high metabolic rate. (vi) Strong flight muscles attached to a keeled sternum, and a crop and gizzard that let the bird eat quickly and digest later. (vii) Absence of a urinary bladder and of most skin glands (only the oil gland at the tail base) further reduce weight.

ncert_questions.q: Could the number of eggs or young ones produced by an oviparous and viviparous mother be equal? Why?
ncert_questions.a: No. An oviparous mother lays eggs outside the body, where they are exposed to predators, unfavourable weather and drying, and receive little or no parental care; many eggs are lost, so she must produce a large number to ensure that a few survive (a frog or a fish lays hundreds to thousands). A viviparous mother retains and nourishes the embryos inside her body, so they develop in a protected environment and are born at an advanced stage, often followed by parental care; the survival rate is high and only a few young are produced at a time. The numbers therefore cannot be equal; the oviparous mother produces far more.

ncert_questions.q: Segmentation in the body is first observed in which of the following: (a) Platyhelminthes (b) Aschelminthes (c) Annelida (d) Arthropoda
ncert_questions.a: (c) Annelida. Metameric segmentation, the division of the body externally and internally into segments with serial repetition of organs, first appears in annelids such as the earthworm. The proglottids of a tapeworm are not true metameres.

ncert_questions.q: Match the following: (a) Operculum (b) Parapodia (c) Scales (d) Comb plates (e) Radula (f) Hairs (g) Choanocytes (h) Gill slits — with (i) Ctenophora (ii) Mollusca (iii) Porifera (iv) Reptilia (v) Annelida (vi) Cyclostomata and Chondrichthyes (vii) Mammalia (viii) Osteichthyes
ncert_questions.a:
(a) Operculum → (viii) Osteichthyes
(b) Parapodia → (v) Annelida
(c) Scales → (iv) Reptilia
(d) Comb plates → (i) Ctenophora
(e) Radula → (ii) Mollusca
(f) Hairs → (vii) Mammalia
(g) Choanocytes → (iii) Porifera
(h) Gill slits → (vi) Cyclostomata and Chondrichthyes

ncert_questions.q: Prepare a list of some animals that are found parasitic on human beings.
ncert_questions.a: Platyhelminthes: Taenia solium (pork tapeworm, intestine), Fasciola hepatica (liver fluke). Aschelminthes: Ascaris lumbricoides (round worm, intestine), Wuchereria bancrofti (filaria worm, lymph vessels, causes elephantiasis), Ancylostoma duodenale (hookworm, intestine), Enterobius (pinworm). Annelida: Hirudinaria (blood-sucking leech, ectoparasite). Arthropoda (ectoparasites and vectors): Pediculus (head louse), Cimex (bed bug), Sarcoptes (itch mite), and the mosquitoes Anopheles, Culex and Aedes, which feed on blood and transmit malaria, filariasis and dengue. Protozoa (from the previous chapter, if asked for parasites in general): Plasmodium (malaria), Entamoeba (amoebic dysentery), Trypanosoma (sleeping sickness).

ncert_questions.q: Differentiate between a polyp and a medusa with one example each.
ncert_questions.a: Polyp: a sessile, cylindrical body form attached at the base with the mouth and tentacles directed upward, reproduces asexually by budding; examples Hydra and Adamsia. Medusa: a free-swimming, umbrella-shaped body form with the mouth on a manubrium directed downward and tentacles around the margin, reproduces sexually by gametes; example Aurelia. In Obelia both forms alternate in one life cycle (metagenesis).

ncert_questions.q: Mention two similarities between (a) Aves and Mammalia, (b) a frog and a crocodile, (c) a turtle and Pila.
ncert_questions.a: (a) Aves and Mammalia: both have a four-chambered heart and are homoiothermous (warm-blooded); both have internal fertilisation and direct development. (b) Frog and crocodile: both are cold-blooded tetrapods with a tympanum representing the ear and a cloaca; both are oviparous. (c) Turtle and Pila: both have a hard protective shell (bony in the turtle, calcareous in Pila); both are oviparous and can withdraw the soft body into the shell.

ncert_questions.q: Excretory organs of different animals are given below. Choose the correct match: flame cells, nephridia, Malpighian tubules, proboscis gland.
ncert_questions.a: Flame cells: Platyhelminthes (Taenia). Nephridia: Annelida (Pheretima). Malpighian tubules: Arthropoda (insects such as Locusta). Proboscis gland: Hemichordata (Balanoglossus).

pyq.q: Which of the following animals shows a pseudocoelom?
pyq.answer: b
pyq.solution: Ascaris belongs to Aschelminthes, the only pseudocoelomate phylum; Fasciola is acoelomate, Pheretima and Asterias are coelomates.

pyq.q: Metagenesis (alternation of polyp and medusa generations) is shown by
pyq.answer: b
pyq.solution: Obelia exists in both polyp and medusa forms; polyps produce medusae asexually and medusae produce polyps sexually. Hydra and Adamsia are polyps only; Pleurobrachia is a ctenophore.

pyq.q: Which one of the following phyla has a complete alimentary canal, a pseudocoelom and sexes separate with the female longer than the male?
pyq.answer: c
pyq.solution: All three features are NCERT statements for Aschelminthes (roundworms).

pyq.q: The excretory organs in Arthropoda and Hemichordata respectively are
pyq.answer: b
pyq.solution: Arthropods excrete through Malpighian tubules; the excretory organ of hemichordates is the proboscis gland.

pyq.q: Which of the following is a living fossil belonging to phylum Arthropoda?
pyq.answer: a
pyq.solution: Limulus, the king crab, is the living fossil in NCERT's arthropod list; Laccifer is the lac insect, Locusta the locust, and Loligo is a mollusc (squid).

pyq.q: In which of the following the adult is radially symmetrical but the larva is bilaterally symmetrical?
pyq.answer: c
pyq.solution: Echinoderms are radial as adults and bilateral as larvae; cnidarians and ctenophores are radial throughout, hemichordates bilateral throughout.

pyq.q: Among the protochordates, the notochord extends from head to tail and persists throughout life in
pyq.answer: b
pyq.solution: Branchiostoma is a cephalochordate, in which the notochord runs from head to tail for life. Ascidia, Salpa and Doliolum are urochordates, in which the notochord is present only in the larval tail.

pyq.q: Which of the following pairs is correctly matched?
pyq.answer: c
pyq.solution: Ornithorhynchus (platypus) is the oviparous mammal. Trygon has a poison sting (Torpedo has the electric organ), Ichthyophis is a limbless amphibian, and Hippocampus is a bony fish.

pyq.q: A four-chambered heart is found in all of the following except
pyq.answer: c
pyq.solution: Calotes is a lizard with a three-chambered heart; crocodiles, birds and mammals have four chambers.

pyq.q: Bioluminescence is well marked in members of phylum
pyq.answer: b
pyq.solution: NCERT states that bioluminescence, the emission of light by a living organism, is well marked in ctenophores such as Pleurobrachia.

pyq.q: Assertion (A): Cartilaginous fishes have to swim constantly to avoid sinking. Reason (R): Cartilaginous fishes lack an air bladder.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
pyq.answer: a
pyq.solution: The air bladder regulates buoyancy in bony fishes; its absence in Chondrichthyes is exactly why they must keep swimming.

pyq.q: Assertion (A): Hemichordata is now placed as a separate phylum under non-chordates. Reason (R): Hemichordates have a proboscis, collar and trunk.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
pyq.answer: b
pyq.solution: Both statements are true, but hemichordates are removed from Chordata because they lack a true notochord, not because of their three body regions.

pyq.q: Assertion (A): All vertebrates are chordates but all chordates are not vertebrates. Reason (R): In vertebrates the notochord is replaced by a vertebral column, whereas protochordates retain the notochord and never develop a vertebral column.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
pyq.answer: a
pyq.solution: The reason gives precisely the distinction that makes urochordates and cephalochordates chordates without being vertebrates.

pyq.q: Assertion (A): Aschelminthes are called pseudocoelomates. Reason (R): In Aschelminthes the body cavity is lined by mesoderm on both the body-wall side and the gut side.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
pyq.answer: c
pyq.solution: The pseudocoelom is not lined by mesoderm; mesoderm is present only as scattered pouches between the ectoderm and endoderm. R describes a true coelom.

pyq.q: Define metameric segmentation. Name the phylum in which it first appears and give one example.
pyq.answer: Metameric segmentation is the division of the body, externally and internally, into a series of segments (metameres) with serial repetition of at least some organs such as nephridia, ganglia and muscles in each segment. It first appears in phylum Annelida; example, the earthworm Pheretima (or Nereis).

pyq.q: Distinguish between open and closed circulatory systems with one example of each.
pyq.answer: In an open circulatory system blood pumped out of the heart leaves the vessels and bathes the cells and tissues directly in body spaces; example Arthropoda (cockroach, prawn) and most Mollusca. In a closed circulatory system blood is circulated only through a series of vessels of varying diameters, arteries, veins and capillaries, and never leaves them; example Annelida (earthworm) and all chordates.

pyq.q: What are cnidoblasts? Mention their functions.
pyq.answer: Cnidoblasts (cnidocytes) are specialised cells of cnidarians, present on the tentacles and the body, that contain a stinging capsule called the nematocyst. Functions: anchorage, defence and capture of prey.

pyq.q: Name the three fundamental characters of phylum Chordata. Which subphylum has the notochord only in the larval tail?
pyq.answer: The three fundamental chordate characters are: (i) a notochord, (ii) a dorsal hollow nerve cord, and (iii) paired pharyngeal gill slits. The notochord is present only in the larval tail in subphylum Urochordata (Tunicata), for example Ascidia.

pyq.q: Give two differences between Chondrichthyes and Osteichthyes.
pyq.answer: (i) Chondrichthyes have a cartilaginous endoskeleton, Osteichthyes a bony one. (ii) Gill slits are separate and without an operculum in Chondrichthyes; in Osteichthyes four pairs of gills are covered by an operculum. (Also acceptable: placoid versus cycloid or ctenoid scales; air bladder absent versus present; ventral versus terminal mouth; internal versus external fertilisation.)

pyq.q: Describe the water transport system of sponges and state its functions.
pyq.answer: Sponges have a water transport or canal system. Water enters through minute pores called ostia in the body wall, flows into the central cavity, the spongocoel, and goes out through a single large opening, the osculum. The spongocoel and the canals are lined by flagellated collar cells, the choanocytes, whose flagella create the current and whose collars trap food particles; digestion is intracellular. Functions of the canal system: (i) gathering food, (ii) respiratory exchange (uptake of oxygen and removal of carbon dioxide) and (iii) removal of waste. Examples: Sycon, Spongilla, Euspongia.

pyq.q: Write the salient features of phylum Echinodermata and name two examples.
pyq.answer: (i) Endoskeleton of calcareous ossicles, hence spiny bodied; all marine; organ-system level of organisation. (ii) Adults radially symmetrical, larvae bilaterally symmetrical; triploblastic and coelomate. (iii) Digestive system complete, mouth on the lower (ventral) side and anus on the upper (dorsal) side. (iv) Water vascular system, the most distinctive feature, helping in locomotion, capture and transport of food, and respiration. (v) Excretory system absent. (vi) Sexes separate; sexual reproduction; fertilisation usually external; indirect development with a free-swimming larva. Examples: Asterias (star fish), Echinus (sea urchin), Antedon (sea lily), Cucumaria (sea cucumber), Ophiura (brittle star).

pyq.q: Compare chordates and non-chordates on any three points, as given in NCERT.
pyq.answer: (i) Notochord: present in chordates; absent in non-chordates. (ii) Central nervous system: dorsal, hollow and single in chordates; ventral, solid and double in non-chordates. (iii) Pharynx: perforated by gill slits in chordates; not perforated in non-chordates. (iv) Heart: ventral in chordates; dorsal, if present, in non-chordates. (v) Post-anal tail: present in chordates; absent in non-chordates. Any three earn full marks.

pyq.q: Give three characters of class Mammalia that are not found in any other class of vertebrates. Name one oviparous and two viviparous mammals.
pyq.answer: Unique mammalian characters: (i) mammary glands (milk-producing glands) to nourish the young; (ii) skin bearing hair; (iii) external ears or pinnae. (Also: different types of teeth in the jaw.) Oviparous mammal: Ornithorhynchus (platypus). Viviparous mammals: Macropus (kangaroo), Pteropus (flying fox), Delphinus (dolphin), Balaenoptera (blue whale), Elephas (elephant), Panthera leo (lion).

pyq.q: Write the salient features of phylum Mollusca with two examples.
pyq.answer: (i) Second largest animal phylum; terrestrial or aquatic (marine or fresh water); organ-system level; bilateral, triploblastic, coelomate. (ii) Body covered by a calcareous shell and unsegmented, with a distinct head, muscular foot and visceral hump. (iii) A soft spongy layer of skin, the mantle, covers the visceral hump; the mantle cavity contains feather-like gills that serve for respiration and excretion. (iv) The head bears sensory tentacles; the mouth has a file-like rasping organ, the radula, for feeding. (v) Usually dioecious, oviparous, with indirect development. Examples: Pila (apple snail), Pinctada (pearl oyster), Sepia (cuttlefish), Octopus (devil fish), Aplysia (sea-hare).

pyq.q: Explain the basis of classification of animals under the heads: levels of organisation, symmetry, germ layers, coelom, segmentation and notochord, with suitable examples.
pyq.answer:
Levels of organisation. Cellular level: cells as loose aggregates (sponges). Tissue level: cells of one function arranged into tissues (coelenterates). Organ level: tissues grouped into organs (Platyhelminthes). Organ-system level: organs form functional systems (annelids to chordates). Organ systems further differ: the digestive system is incomplete (single opening, Platyhelminthes) or complete (mouth and anus); circulation is open (blood bathes tissues directly, arthropods) or closed (blood in vessels, annelids, chordates).

Symmetry. Asymmetrical: no plane gives equal halves (sponges). Radial: any plane through the central axis gives identical halves (coelenterates, ctenophores, echinoderms). Bilateral: only one plane gives identical halves (annelids, arthropods and higher phyla).

Germ layers. Diploblastic: two embryonic layers, ectoderm and endoderm, with undifferentiated mesoglea between (coelenterates). Triploblastic: a third layer, mesoderm, between them (Platyhelminthes to chordates).

Coelom. A body cavity lined by mesoderm. Coelomates: annelids, molluscs, arthropods, echinoderms, hemichordates, chordates. Pseudocoelomates: cavity not lined by mesoderm, mesoderm as scattered pouches (Aschelminthes). Acoelomates: no body cavity (Platyhelminthes).

Segmentation. Body divided externally and internally into segments with serial repetition of organs, metameric segmentation, as in the earthworm; first in Annelida.

Notochord. A mesodermally derived rod on the dorsal side formed during embryonic development. Present: chordates. Absent: non-chordates (Porifera to Echinodermata and Hemichordata). Draw the coelom cross-sections and the symmetry figure alongside.

pyq.q: Give an outline classification of phylum Chordata up to classes, mentioning one distinguishing feature and one example for each subphylum and class.
pyq.answer: Chordata (notochord, dorsal hollow nerve cord, paired pharyngeal gill slits) has three subphyla. Urochordata: notochord only in the larval tail; Ascidia, Salpa, Doliolum. Cephalochordata: notochord from head to tail throughout life; Branchiostoma. Both are protochordates and exclusively marine. Vertebrata: notochord replaced by a vertebral column; ventral muscular heart, kidneys, paired appendages. Vertebrata is divided into division Agnatha (jawless), class Cyclostomata: circular sucking mouth without jaws, 6–15 pairs of gill slits, ectoparasites on fishes; Petromyzon, Myxine; and division Gnathostomata (jawed), with superclass Pisces (fins) and superclass Tetrapoda (limbs). Pisces: class Chondrichthyes, cartilaginous endoskeleton, no operculum, placoid scales, no air bladder; Scoliodon, Pristis. Class Osteichthyes, bony endoskeleton, operculum, air bladder; Labeo, Hippocampus. Tetrapoda: class Amphibia, moist scaleless skin, three-chambered heart, external fertilisation, indirect development; Rana, Bufo. Class Reptilia, dry cornified skin with scales, three-chambered heart (four in crocodiles), internal fertilisation; Naja, Chelone. Class Aves, feathers, wings, pneumatic bones, four-chambered heart, warm-blooded, oviparous; Columba, Struthio. Class Mammalia, mammary glands, hair, pinnae, four-chambered heart, warm-blooded, viviparous (except Ornithorhynchus); Macropus, Balaenoptera. Present the answer as a flow chart plus this list.

pyq.q: Describe the characteristic features of phylum Arthropoda. Why is it regarded as the largest phylum? Give examples of arthropods under the heads economically important, vectors, gregarious pest and living fossil.
pyq.answer:
Features. Organ-system level; bilaterally symmetrical, triploblastic, segmented, coelomate. Body covered by a chitinous exoskeleton and divided into head, thorax and abdomen. Jointed appendages. Respiratory organs gills, book gills, book lungs or tracheal system. Open circulatory system. Sensory organs: antennae, compound and simple eyes, statocysts (balance organs). Excretion through Malpighian tubules. Mostly dioecious; fertilisation usually internal; mostly oviparous; development direct or indirect.

Largest phylum. Over two-thirds of all named species are arthropods, because the exoskeleton protects and prevents water loss, jointed appendages allow varied locomotion and feeding, insects can fly, the small size lets many species share a habitat, diverse respiratory organs suit every habitat, sense organs are well developed, reproductive capacity is high, and metamorphosis prevents competition between larva and adult.

Examples. Economically important insects: Apis (honey bee), Bombyx (silkworm), Laccifer (lac insect). Vectors: Anopheles, Culex and Aedes (mosquitoes). Gregarious pest: Locusta (locust). Living fossil: Limulus (king crab).

pyq.q:
A student collects a marine animal that is transparent, oval, radially symmetrical and diploblastic, with eight rows of ciliated plates on its outer surface. At night it glows. It has a gastro-vascular cavity, reproduces only sexually and its embryo develops into a larva.
(i) Identify the phylum and name one example.
(ii) What is the function of the ciliated plates and what are they called?
(iii) Name the property by which the animal glows.
(iv) State two features that distinguish this phylum from Coelenterata.
pyq.answer: (i) Phylum Ctenophora (comb jellies or sea walnuts); example Pleurobrachia or Ctenoplana. (ii) The plates are comb plates; they help in locomotion. (iii) Bioluminescence, the property of a living organism to emit light. (iv) Ctenophores have comb plates and no cnidoblasts (cnidarians have cnidoblasts with nematocysts and no comb plates); ctenophores reproduce only sexually with no polyp-medusa alternation, whereas many cnidarians show both asexual budding and metagenesis; ctenophores are exclusively marine while some cnidarians (Hydra) live in fresh water.

pyq.q:
Read the passage and answer. The coelom is a body cavity lined by mesoderm. Its presence and nature is important in classification. Some animals have no body cavity; in some the cavity is not lined by mesoderm and the mesoderm lies as scattered pouches; in others the cavity is lined by mesoderm on both sides. Four animals are given: Taenia, Ascaris, Nereis, Rana.
(i) Classify each of the four animals as acoelomate, pseudocoelomate or coelomate.
(ii) In which of these animals is the body cavity not lined by mesoderm, and what is such a cavity called?
(iii) Name the phylum in which a true coelom appears for the first time in NCERT order.
(iv) Why is the coelom found only in triploblastic animals?
pyq.answer: (i) Taenia, acoelomate (Platyhelminthes); Ascaris, pseudocoelomate (Aschelminthes); Nereis, coelomate (Annelida); Rana, coelomate (Chordata). (ii) Ascaris; the cavity is a pseudocoelom, with the mesoderm present only as scattered pouches between the ectoderm and endoderm. (iii) Annelida. (iv) The coelom is by definition lined by mesoderm; diploblastic animals have only ectoderm and endoderm with a non-cellular mesoglea between, so they cannot form a mesoderm-lined cavity.

common_mistakes: Writing 'mesoderm' for diploblastic animals. Coelenterates have a non-cellular mesoglea between ectoderm and endoderm; mesoderm appears only in triploblastic animals, and the examiner treats the two words as different answers.
Defining the coelom as 'a body cavity'. The marking scheme wants 'lined by mesoderm'; without that phrase the definition also fits a pseudocoelom and earns no mark.

Calling echinoderms radially symmetrical without qualification. The adult is radial and the larva bilateral; the qualification is a marking point and the reason the phylum sits with bilateral animals.
Reversing the direction of metagenesis. In Obelia the polyp produces the medusa asexually and the medusa produces the polyp sexually; writing it the other way round loses the mark.

Mixing up the excretory organs: flame cells belong to Platyhelminthes, nephridia to Annelida, Malpighian tubules to Arthropoda, the proboscis gland to Hemichordata. Echinoderms have no excretory system.
Giving the reptile heart as simply three-chambered. Write 'usually three-chambered, four-chambered in crocodiles'; the exception is what is tested.

Placing examples in the wrong group: Limulus (king crab) is an arthropod, Aplysia and Dentalium are molluscs, Ichthyophis is an amphibian, Hippocampus is a bony fish, Pteropus, Delphinus and Balaenoptera are mammals, Aptenodytes is a bird.

Answering 'peculiar features of parasitic platyhelminthes' with the general features of the phylum. The question wants hooks and suckers, direct absorption of nutrients through the body surface and the flattened body.

Listing the two-chambered heart, cold-bloodedness or the streamlined body as differences between Chondrichthyes and Osteichthyes. These are shared; the differences are skeleton, mouth position, operculum, scales, air bladder and fertilisation.
Forgetting Hemichordata when listing non-chordate phyla, or still placing it under Chordata. The rationalised NCERT treats it as the tenth non-chordate phylum.
strategy:
Treat this chapter as two halves and prepare them differently. The first half, section 4.1, is concept: six characters (level of organisation, symmetry, germ layers, coelom, segmentation, notochord). Learn each with its definition in NCERT words, one example on each side, and the three figures (symmetry, germ layers, coelom cross-sections). This half gives the 5-mark question and most of the Assertion–Reason items, so practise writing the full basis-of-classification answer once with diagrams and time yourself at ten minutes.

The second half is memory. Make one table with eleven phylum rows and these columns: level of organisation, symmetry, germ layers, coelom, digestive system, circulation, respiratory organ, excretory organ, sexes, fertilisation, development, two examples. Fill it from NCERT, not from a guide, and revise the table rather than the text. Then make a second table for the seven vertebrate classes with columns: skeleton, skin covering, mouth or beak, respiration, heart chambers, temperature, fertilisation, oviparous or viviparous, development, three examples. The 'firsts' (first complete gut, first coelom, first closed circulation) and the 'special one-liners' from the formula sheet are the MCQ bank; read them aloud twice.

Examples decide the odd-one-out questions. Learn the examples in NCERT's own groupings (economic insects, vectors, marine versus fresh water fishes, poisonous snakes, oviparous versus viviparous mammals) because the examiner sets the question from the grouping. Write all fifteen NCERT exercise answers once; exercises 6, 7, 9, 10, 11 and 12 are asked almost verbatim. Draw Sycon, Hydra, Ascaris, Asterias, Balanoglossus and Branchiostoma with labels at least once each. In the exam, answer the salient-features questions as numbered points, one feature per line, and always end with two examples: that is how the marking scheme is written.
